name: Coalition Diversification
consequences: Pulling this lever expands the stakeholder base beyond civil society to include industry, academia, and private security firms, increasing legitimacy but potentially introducing conflicting interests and slower decision cycles.
options: Engage a cross‑sector advisory board that meets quarterly to align objectives across civil society, academia, and industry.
Launch a public consultation portal inviting feedback from all digital identity stakeholders to capture diverse perspectives.
Partner with a neutral think‑tank to mediate between divergent interests and synthesize a unified position.
review: Expanding coalition increases influence but risks diluting focus and creating internal conflict; it leaves the challenge of maintaining a coherent advocacy narrative unaddressed.

name: Regulatory Framing
consequences: Reframing the dependency issue as a resilience and continuity risk shifts policy attention from privacy to strategic autonomy, potentially accelerating procurement changes but may trigger pushback from incumbent vendors who argue cost and stability.
options: Draft a policy brief that quantifies continuity risks using scenario analysis of platform outages.
Host a policy workshop with procurement officials to embed resilience metrics into future tender criteria.
Publish a comparative study of sovereign identity models from other EU members to benchmark best practices.
review: Framing as resilience attracts procurement focus but may provoke vendor resistance; it leaves the gap of quantifying cost trade‑offs unaddressed.

name: Demonstrator Portfolio
consequences: Developing two distinct non‑production demonstrators showcases feasibility of fallback paths, building technical credibility but consumes limited resources that could otherwise be spent on policy advocacy.
options: Build a GrapheneOS‑based mobile demo that authenticates via FIDO2/WebAuthn against a mock IDP for testing scenarios.
Create a browser‑based fallback demo using hardware tokens and OpenID Connect to simulate a platform‑neutral flow.
Prototype a low‑cost hardware token prototype that can be distributed to key stakeholders for hands‑on testing.
review: Demonstrators prove technical feasibility but divert budget from advocacy; they leave the gap of scaling demonstrations to production environments unaddressed.

name: Procurement Language
consequences: Embedding platform‑neutral clauses into AltID procurement documents can lock in future designs, but may face legal and procedural hurdles that delay adoption.
options: Draft procurement specifications that mandate exclusion of Apple/Google integrity APIs in all future eIDAS‑aligned wallets.
Propose a clause requiring a certified fallback authentication path in all future eIDAS‑aligned wallets for critical public services.
Offer a template for a “platform‑neutral” addendum that can be appended to existing tender documents.
review: Adding procurement language can enforce neutrality but may stall procurement cycles; it leaves the gap of ensuring enforceability of the clauses unaddressed.

name: EU Standards Alignment
consequences: Aligning Danish advocacy with EU Digital Identity Wallet standards amplifies influence but may require aligning with broader EU timelines and competing national interests, potentially diluting Denmark’s specific goals.
options: Contribute to the EU Digital Identity Wallet working group with a Danish platform‑neutral position paper.
Coordinate with other EU members to co‑author a joint request for platform‑neutral language in the next EU standard draft.
Host an EU‑level roundtable to discuss fallback mechanisms and secure a consensus statement for future policy development.
review: EU alignment raises profile but may clash with national priorities; it leaves the gap of translating EU language into national procurement unaddressed.

name: Contingency Planning
consequences: Formalizing a contingency plan for platform disruptions builds resilience but may be perceived as alarmist, potentially reducing stakeholder buy‑in and diverting resources from proactive measures.
options: Develop a tabletop exercise scenario that simulates a sudden Apple/Google policy change and tests fallback flows.
Publish a risk register that maps potential platform failure modes and mitigation actions for stakeholder preparedness.
Create a rapid‑response task force that can mobilize stakeholders during an actual platform outage to ensure service continuity.
review: Contingency planning enhances readiness but risks alarmism; it leaves the gap of ensuring stakeholder engagement during real outages unaddressed.

name: Platform Integrity Signal Decoupling
consequences: Pulling this lever reduces reliance on Apple/Google integrity APIs, but requires developing alternative trust anchors and may increase integration complexity for existing services. The new anchors must be certified across all public services, adding a layer of regulatory scrutiny.
options: Build a national integrity verification service that validates device state via open hardware attestation for public services across the ministry.
Leverage existing open‑source OS‑level integrity checks (e.g., GrapheneOS) and certify them for public use across services.
Partner with a neutral hardware manufacturer to embed a tamper‑evident chip that reports device integrity to the identity stack.
review: Decoupling integrity signals cuts vendor lock‑in but introduces the risk of fragmented trust anchors that may be harder to certify across all public services.

name: Open‑Source Trust Anchor Development
consequences: Creating an open‑source trust anchor increases transparency and community scrutiny, but may slow adoption due to perceived lower maturity and support. The anchor must be maintained and audited to meet public‑sector security standards.
options: Release a modular, community‑reviewed library that implements FIDO2 attestation for any OS across all public services.
Host a public bug‑bounty program to accelerate security hardening of the trust anchor across all deployments.
Integrate the library into a national security‑grade sandbox environment to demonstrate resilience for all citizen services.
review: Open‑source anchors boost transparency yet risk slower uptake and potential fragmentation of support across agencies, delaying widespread deployment in critical services.

name: Cross‑Platform Credential Portability
consequences: Enabling credential portability across OSes expands user choice, but requires harmonizing credential formats and may increase the attack surface. Compliance tracking becomes more complex across agencies.
options: Standardize a universal credential schema that maps to both FIDO2 and WebAuthn across platforms for all public services.
Deploy a middleware gateway that translates platform‑specific credentials into a common format for public services.
Introduce a policy that mandates credential export/import capabilities for all citizen devices across all services.
review: Portability enhances choice but may broaden attack vectors and complicate compliance tracking, increasing audit overhead for public agencies and stretching resource limits.

name: Stakeholder Engagement Cadence
consequences: Establishing a regular engagement cadence keeps stakeholders aligned, but consumes significant time and may dilute focus on technical deliverables. The cadence must be disciplined to avoid scope creep.
options: Schedule quarterly round‑table workshops with civil‑society, academia, and industry to co‑create policy drafts for procurement.
Create a digital liaison portal where stakeholders submit feedback and receive real‑time status updates for all project milestones.
Appoint a dedicated stakeholder liaison officer to coordinate outreach and synthesize input across all stakeholder groups.
review: Regular engagement fosters alignment but risks diverting resources from core technical milestones, potentially delaying demonstrator development and procurement readiness, and reducing budget flexibility.

name: Alternative Distribution Channels
consequences: Diversifying distribution channels reduces dependency on app stores, but introduces security vetting challenges and user adoption friction. The channels must be secure and user‑friendly to gain acceptance.
options: Deploy a secure, government‑managed app distribution portal with signed binaries for all public services across the ministry.
Use QR‑code‑based installation on pre‑loaded trusted devices to bypass app stores for all citizen applications.
Leverage a certified hardware token that embeds the identity app and can be distributed via postal service.
review: Alternative channels lower store dependence but add vetting overhead and may hinder user convenience, potentially reducing adoption rates among older citizens.

name: Hardware Token Integration
consequences: Integrating hardware tokens offers a platform‑neutral fallback, but increases procurement costs and requires user education. Adoption may be uneven across demographic groups.
options: Issue a national e‑ID token that bundles authentication and attestation functions for all services across the public sector.
Partner with a neutral hardware vendor to produce low‑cost, reusable tokens for citizens across all service portals.
Pilot a mobile‑SIM‑based token that leverages existing telecom infrastructure for authentication across all citizen devices.
review: Tokens provide fallback resilience but raise cost and adoption barriers that may limit scalability, especially in low‑income regions lacking compatible hardware.

name: Supplier Concentration Mitigation
consequences: Pulling this lever reduces reliance on Apple and Google by encouraging alternative app distribution and device trust models. This may increase complexity for developers and require new certification pathways. Downstream, potential delays in adoption and higher initial integration costs may arise.
options: Mandate that all future Danish eID apps must support a secondary open‑source OS distribution channel, requiring developers to publish binaries for a privacy‑focused Android fork.
Require public sector vendors to submit a supplier diversification scorecard, penalizing contracts that exceed a threshold of foreign platform dependency.
Create a government‑backed certification program for third‑party app stores that meet Danish security standards, enabling alternative distribution without compromising trust.
review: Mandating alternative distribution channels adds developer overhead and may slow rollout, while the options do not directly address the need for a robust fallback authentication mechanism during platform outages.

name: Fallback Authentication Architecture
consequences: Establishing a fallback architecture provides a platform‑neutral path for critical services, reducing continuity risk. It may introduce additional authentication steps for users and require new backend integration, potentially impacting user experience and system performance.
options: Design a modular authentication gateway that can switch between primary mobile OS signals and a hardware‑token based fallback, with automatic failover triggered by OS integrity checks.
Deploy a browser‑based WebAuthn portal that accepts biometric credentials stored locally, bypassing mobile OS integrity APIs entirely.
Integrate a secure enclave on government servers that can validate signed challenge responses from any device, eliminating reliance on platform‑specific trust signals.
review: Building a fallback gateway increases system complexity and may degrade performance, yet the options leave the question of how to maintain user privacy and data minimization across multiple authentication channels.

name: Procurement Language Standardization
consequences: Standardizing procurement language forces suppliers to disclose platform dependencies and include fallback clauses, tightening control over future contracts. It may raise procurement cycle times and require legal review, potentially delaying procurement decisions.
options: Introduce a mandatory clause in all eID procurement documents that specifies exclusion of exclusive reliance on Apple or Google integrity APIs.
Require that all vendor proposals include a quantified risk assessment of platform lock‑in, with penalties for exceeding acceptable thresholds.
Adopt a template procurement brief that embeds a fallback authentication requirement, mandating proof of platform‑neutral access before contract award.
review: Standardizing procurement language can slow procurement cycles, and the options do not directly solve the challenge of verifying that fallback mechanisms are operational during crises.

name: Stakeholder Advocacy Momentum
consequences: Amplifying advocacy builds political pressure for platform neutrality, potentially accelerating policy change. It may divert resources from technical work and risk political backlash if perceived as anti‑technology.
options: Launch a coordinated media campaign highlighting the sovereignty risks of platform dependence, targeting both policymakers and the public.
Organize a series of round‑table workshops with civil‑society, academia, and industry to co‑create a platform‑neutral policy brief.
Secure endorsements from key parliamentary committees by presenting evidence of platform lock‑in risks in a formal briefing.
review: Advocacy efforts may consume significant time and risk political pushback, and the options do not directly address the technical feasibility of fallback solutions.

name: Technical Proof of Concept Validation
consequences: Validating proof‑of‑concepts demonstrates feasibility and builds credibility with stakeholders. It may consume resources that could otherwise be spent on policy or procurement work, and may not scale to production.
options: Build a lightweight FIDO2/WebAuthn demonstrator on GrapheneOS that authenticates against a mock Danish eID server, showing platform‑neutral capability.
Develop a browser‑based fallback using WebAuthn and a local credential store, proving that users can authenticate without mobile OS signals.
Create a hardware‑token prototype that can be used in place of mobile devices, validating that token‑based fallback is viable for critical services.
review: Demonstrator development can divert resources from policy work, and the options do not guarantee that the prototypes will meet production security and compliance standards.

name: EU Standards Alignment Lever
consequences: Aligning with EU Digital Identity Wallet standards embeds platform neutrality into broader European policy, increasing legitimacy and potential funding. It may require extensive coordination with EU bodies and delay national initiatives.
options: Submit a formal position paper to the European Digital Identity Working Group advocating for mandatory fallback authentication in all member‑state wallets.
Participate in EU standardization meetings to propose a new interoperability profile that excludes platform‑specific integrity checks.
Collaborate with other Nordic countries to draft a joint EU submission that emphasizes regional sovereignty and platform‑neutral design.
review: EU engagement can be slow and may not influence national procurement timelines, while the options do not directly address Denmark’s immediate platform‑neutral procurement needs.

name: Resilience Framing Campaign
consequences: Framing platform dependence as a resilience risk reframes the debate from privacy to national security, potentially gaining broader support. It may also polarize stakeholders and oversimplify technical nuances.
options: Publish a risk assessment report that quantifies potential service outages if Apple or Google suspend integrity APIs, linking to national security impacts.
Develop a public dashboard that visualizes supplier concentration and platform lock‑in across all eID services, making the risk tangible.
Host a national resilience symposium that brings together security experts, policymakers, and vendors to discuss fallback strategies and continuity plans.
review: Resilience framing can polarize stakeholders and oversimplify technical details, and the options do not directly provide a mechanism for verifying fallback readiness during actual outages.
